newsitem.title: FRANCE: Boeing merger forces Europe to decide on Airbus.
newsitem.headline: Boeing merger forces Europe to decide on Airbus.

text.p: A European Union decision on Wednesday to allow in principle a $15 billion merger of Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp avoided a trade war but forces European politicians to make tough choices.

French politicians in particular have to act swiftly on the restructuring of state-owned Aerospatiale in order to allow the Airbus Industrie plane-making consortium to become a real company with its own capital and balance sheet.
These decisions are all the more sensitive because some industrialists want to use the civil aerospace Airbus grouping as a base for a military industry restructuring as well.
At stake are issues such as national pride and many thousands of aerospace jobs.

French President Jacques Chirac, in line with his staunch Gaullist stance and careful not to be upstaged by the United States in a touchy relationship, had said that the aerospace merger was "extremely dangerous" for the European industry.
Earlier on Wednesday, Chirac and Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin urged the European Commission to be "firm" with Boeing.

Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan on Tuesday night expressed his concerns about the ongoing talks. "I certainly trust that the presumption that commentators put forward that we are on the way to some kind of trade war because of this dispute will be mistaken," he told a House subcommittee during his Humphrey Hawkins testimony.
After the decision was announced on Wednesday, the White House expressed its pleasure and was quick to deny that it forced Boeing into concessions to avoid a trans-Atlantic diplomatic spat.
"We were not holding a gun to their head. No one forced Boeing to do this," an official said.

In Germany, Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said he was happy a trade war had been avoided. "I am happy that the threatened trade conflict between Europe and the U.S. could be avoided through last-minute concessions by Boeing," he said in a statement.
He said Boeing would despite the concessions dominate the world aerospace industry which made it necessary for the four-nation Airbus consortium to restructure.
"The first step must be a reorganisation of Airbus Industrie from a loose consortium to a unified corporation, at best in the form of a public company," he said.

France, Britain, Germany and Spain agree on the need for a single corporate entity for Airbus. The four constituent companies -- Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace GMBH (DASA) and CASA also agree on the principle.
But they do not agree on the scope of the activities for the Airbus group, on the assets to transfer to the new Airbus and on the price of the assets.

British Aerospace managing director John Weston earlier this month told a French parliamentary commission about his idea of a big defence merger of BAe, DASA and Aerospatiale, a plan DASA called desirable but difficult to realise in the short term.

The Boeing concessions to the European Union on Wednesday also had a military component. The company said it would license patents obtained under U.S. funded military contracts to commercial plane manufacturers.
In France, the previous government aimed at a merger between Aerospatiale and combat-plane maker Dassault Aviation.

It also wanted to restructure the defence industry around Thomson-CSF, planning to sell the state's 58-percent stake in the defence electronics group to either Lagardere Groupe or to Alcatel Alsthom with Dassault.

The left-wing government elected six weeks ago is reviewing these issues. It has said it is willing to let its stake in Thomson-CSF fall to below 50 percent but has so far not indicated its plans for Aerospatiale.
For the Airbus merger to go ahead, France must give up its full ownership of Aerospatiale or at least of production assets belonging to the group.
Both BAe's Weston and DASA's Manfred Bischoff have made clear that a privatisation of the French company was not a pre-condition to international cooperation, but would make it easier.

"It would be very difficult for the management of BAe to propose to their sharehodlers to exchange the control of 100 percent of their company against a fraction of a European company in which a state would have a major stake," Weston told French politicians recently.
